title: Jonah and the House
premise: Odile Joubert, a hospice nurse who hears the dying count backwards, returns to the village of Saint-Aubin-le-Froid to settle their grandmother's house and discovers the church bell — melted down in 1911 — ringing again each night at frost. The bell's song is a ledger: it names the descendants of the men who drowned a woman named Marguerite in the well in 1910, and it will not stop until every debt is sung. Odile, whose family name is on that list, must learn the song's forbidden last verse from the dying and the dead without ever singing along, because those who join the chorus are taken to finish the pattern in the ice. In the end Odile sings the verse alone, willingly, trading their place among the living for the village's release — and wakes on the frozen well's edge with the bell silent, the frost finished, and one white streak in their hair that never melts.
about_author: Gideon Lockridge is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing church dissolution records across rural France before turning to fiction. They live near the coast with two deaf cats and an unexplained fondness for bells.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: POV Odile. In the hospice, Odile tends a dying man who counts backwards from nineteen and hums a tune no one taught him; when he reaches zero he whispers 'the bell remembers.' Odile dismisses it as terminal lucidity, but takes the melody home and finds themselves humming it while doing dishes. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Letters from a Cold Solicitor
chapters.summary: POV Odile. A solicitor's letter summons Odile to Saint-Aubin-le-Froid: grandmother Élise Joubert is dead, the house must be settled by first frost. Odile resists returning — seven years of carefully explained noises began there as a child. A second letter arrives already opened, containing only a pressed sprig of frost-burnt yew. Emotional beat: dread of homecoming.

chapters.title: The House That Was Left Running
chapters.summary: POV Odile. The house is warm, lamps lit, a kettle still faintly hot — as if Élise stepped out minutes ago. Odile finds a notebook of backwards numbers dated across decades, ending yesterday. That night, floorboards creak in a rhythm suspiciously like footsteps keeping time to a hymn. Emotional beat: grief curdling into surveillance.

chapters.title: A Village That Won't Say Her Name
chapters.summary: POV Odile. At the tavern, Odile asks about the church bell; the room goes quiet. Old Thérèse Vasseur mutters that the bell was melted in 1911 and 'what rings now isn't bronze.' The mayor offers money to have the house cleared quickly and quietly. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being the only one asking questions.

chapters.title: Nineteen Ten
chapters.summary: POV Odile, with archival fragments. In the ruined presbytery Odile finds parish records: a woman, Marguerite Solane, accused of poisoning cattle, drowned in the village well in November 1910 by nine masked men. The bell was recast from her funeral bell and then melted entirely the following spring. Emotional beat: history arriving like cold water.

chapters.title: The First Ringing
chapters.summary: POV Odile. At midnight the bell rings — though the tower holds nothing but pigeons and rusted yokes. Every villager stands in their doorway, listening, faces lit by candlelight they pretend not to hold. Odile realizes the whole village has been waiting for someone else to hear it first. Emotional beat: shared complicity acknowledged.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile visits the village's last hospice patient, ninety-six-year-old Aurélien, who recognizes the backwards counting: 'We counted her down the well. Nineteen feet.' He gives Odile the song's first verses but refuses the last: 'The last verse is a door. Don't learn it unless you mean to open it.' Emotional beat: confession without absolution.

chapters.title: Names in the Frost
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Morning frost on the kitchen window forms nine names — the descendants' names, including JOUBERT. Each night one name darkens, weeps condensation, then vanishes; the next day, that person falls ill or dies. Odile understands the bell is working down a list, and theirs is seventh. Emotional beat: the horror of inheritance.

chapters.title: Thérèse's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Thérèse Vasseur. The old woman reveals she has kept the village's pact since 1962: leave offerings at the well, never speak Marguerite's name aloud, let the bell take one descendant per generation and call it pneumonia. She begs Odile to accept the role quietly. Emotional beat: loyalty to tradition versus the truth Odile carries.

chapters.title: The Well Breathes
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile opens the sealed well-house behind the church. The air inside moves against the wind, exhaling warmth that smells of tallow and wet wool. Down in the dark, water rises and falls in rhythm — someone breathing, or counting. Odile flees but brings away a button from Marguerite's era caught in the doorframe. Emotional beat: trespass and its immediate price.

chapters.title: Sister Camille's Tape
chapters.summary: POV Odile. A young priest, Camille Ferreol, secretly recorded the bell's song and slowed the tape: beneath the tolling are voices, women's voices, singing a lullaby in old Occitan. Camille believes the bell isn't cursing the village — it's testifying, and the frost-patterns are a legal document written in ice. Emotional beat: hope that the haunting wants justice, not blood.

chapters.title: The Verse Nobody Wrote Down
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Cross-referencing Élise's notebook with Camille's tape, Odile reconstructs five of six verses. The sixth exists only in the memories of the dying — and everyone who has ever learned it sang along and was taken. Élise, Odile realizes, spent her life learning to listen without joining. Emotional beat: understanding the grandmother too late.

chapters.title: One Name Fewer
chapters.summary: POV Odile. The fifth name vanishes from the window; its owner, a schoolteacher, is found standing in the frozen fountain, alive but singing the lullaby in a voice not her own, unable to stop. The village demands Odile leave before drawing the bell's attention further. Emotional beat: the community choosing sacrifice over salvation.

chapters.title: Élise's Room
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Behind the wardrobe Odile finds Élise's true work: forty years of transcriptions, wax-cylinder recordings, and a letter beginning 'If you are reading this, you are the seventh, and I am sorry I taught you silence instead of the song.' Enclosed: instructions for hearing the last verse safely — through another mouth. Emotional beat: inherited love expressed as inherited burden.

chapters.title: The Mouth of the Well
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Following Élise's instructions, Odile holds the button over the open well at midnight and listens. From below, Marguerite's voice — or something wearing it — teaches the final verse slowly, patiently, kindly, which is somehow worse. Odile writes it down phonetically, refusing to shape a single syllable aloud. Emotional beat: tenderness weaponized.

chapters.title: Camille Breaks the Pact
chapters.summary: POV Camille Ferreol. Unable to bear the injustice, Camille plays the complete song — all six verses — over the church loudspeaker, forcing the whole village to hear the testimony. The bell answers with fury: every frost-pane in Saint-Aubin shatters inward, and Camille's own name appears on the list, ninth and last. Emotional beat: righteous defiance triggering catastrophe.

chapters.title: The Night of Nine Bells
chapters.summary: POV Odile. The bell rings continuously; the temperature plummets; the well-house doors stand open and the breath inside is now audible across the square. Villagers gather, some kneeling, some fleeing toward the coast road that fills with fog behind them. Thérèse, dying, tells Odile: 'Finish it properly. Sing it alone, or it will sing itself through all of us.' Emotional beat: siege, and clarity within it.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile confronts what loyalty means: to the grandmother who protected them with silence, to the village that protected itself with sacrifice, to Marguerite who has waited a century for witnesses. The frost writes its final pattern across the square — a scale, a well, a woman's outline — and begins closing like a hand. Emotional beat: decision crystallizing.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Odile. At the well's edge, Odile sings the sixth verse alone — deliberately, fully, naming Marguerite Solane aloud and offering the Joubert debt in full. The song completes; the bell tolls once, sweetly, like a verdict read. The cold rushes inward, and Odile steps into the pattern as it closes. Emotional beat: willing surrender as the only honest act.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: POV Odile, disoriented. Inside the pattern, Odile experiences the counting backwards — nineteen feet of water, the year 1910, Marguerite's actual voice, tired and human, thanking them not for saving her but for hearing her. The choice is offered: stay and keep the ledger company, or carry the last verse back and let it end. Emotional beat: grace in the dark.

chapters.title: First Thaw
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile wakes on the well's edge at dawn, the village silent, the bell tower empty and finally just empty. The frost has written its final pattern and released it: nine names restored to the window, then fading like breath off glass. Camille survives, changed; the schoolteacher stops singing; Thérèse dies peacefully mid-sentence, smiling. Emotional beat: exhausted, unearned-feeling mercy.

chapters.title: The White Streak
chapters.summary: POV Odile, months later. Odile stays in Saint-Aubin, keeps the house, and works as the village's nurse. In the hospice, the dying no longer count backwards — they simply say a woman's name, gently, and are answered by silence that feels like company. One white streak in Odile's hair never warms, and on frost mornings, Odile hums the first five verses only, and always, always stops. Emotional beat: peace that keeps its scar.
